Utilizing Time-slicing to Optimize Inference Throughput

Introduction

The Broadcom Performance team has completed extensive performance tests demonstrating VCF’s efficiency and flexibility for running AI workloads in various configurations. To explain our results, we’ve published a white paper and a series of four blogs:

  • Part 1: Maximizing Performance, Efficiency, and Flexibility in Multi-tenant Environment
  • Part 2: Maximizing GPU Utilization for Best Total Cost of Ownership
  • Part 3: Maximizing CPU and Memory Utilization for Best Total Cost of Ownership
  • Part 4 (this blog post): Utilizing Time-Slicing to Optimize Inference Throughput

Today we are happy to share with you part 4 of this series.

This blog explores how NVIDIA vGPU on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) optimizes GPU utilization by using time-slicing. Unlike traditional partitioning, this approach allows virtualized workloads to, in some cases, outperform bare-metal configurations by intelligently sharing compute resources.

Time-Sliced vGPU vs. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) 

There are two primary ways to share GPU resources in a virtualized environment. Both approaches isolate memory. They differ on the axis that determines everything: whether compute cores are partitioned or scheduled. 

Why this matters: MIG vGPU’s rigid boundaries prevent one workload from using another’s spare capacity. vGPU’s round-robin scheduler still guarantees each VM a minimum allotment, but lets it exceed that allotment whenever a neighbor skips its turn. 

The “Time-Slicing” Advantage:

The core innovation lies in spreading a workload’s vGPU profiles across more physical GPUs than strictly necessary for its memory requirements. The workload then absorbs compute cycles its neighbors leave idle — beating bare metal on aggregate throughput (our testing showed 30% better than bare metal on models from Hugging-Face, 10% better than bare metal for models compiled with TRT-LLM). The gain scales with slack; the less optimized the model, the more idle cycles exist to reclaim.

Figure 1: Three different placements of the workloads: 1x Llama4 17B, and 4x Mistral 7B. 

The classic placement (“Layout A”) has a total of five VMs: one running Llama4 17B and four VMs running Mistral 7B. The Llama4 17B model uses three physical GPUs and the Mistral models share the fourth GPU. 

The novel placement (“Layout B”) exploits time-slicing. In Layout B, the Llama4 17B spreads its vGPUs over all four physical GPUs, and the Mistral workload spreads over the two physical GPUs that have GPU memory available. If all four GPUs had GPU memory available, we could have spread the Mistral over all four GPUs. Layout B allows a workload to use compute cycles that are not being used by another workload on the same GPU. This results in higher aggregate throughput than with Layout A. Since NVIDIA vGPU on VCF uses time-slices that are assigned round-robin to the VMs, no workload will be starved of compute resources. Every workload is guaranteed a minimum compute allotment, but can receive more if another workload is not using its time slice. 

The third placement (“Layout C”) has only one VM on ESX (or runs without VMs on bare metal). Layout C assigns all four NVIDIA A100-80C GPUs to every container; i.e., the containers share the GPUs. Layout C does not support pre-emption, so a workload that uses only one GPU could starve a workload that needs all the GPUs. In addition to being unfair, it also leaves plenty of GPU compute unused.

Layout B allows a workload to claim as much GPU compute as possible while only reserving the minimum GPU memory necessary. It is particularly effective for embarrassingly parallel workloads, such as:

  • LLM Inference: e.g., Llama 3/4, Mistral.
  • Financial Analytics: High-performance computing (HPC) tasks, such as “computing the Greeks.”

Where the extra throughput comes from: A single GPU’s compute cycles, before and after the change in VM-to-GPU assignment. Nothing is added to the machine; previously stranded capacity simply becomes reachable. 

Figure 2: A conceptual illustration of round-robin slice reallocation. This is not measured data.

How the scheduler behaves:

  • Slices are handed to VMs round-robin, so no workload is ever starved. Each keeps a guaranteed minimum compute allotment. 
  • When Llama4 is between batches and skips its turn, Mistral runs in that window instead of the GPU sitting idle. 
  • The effect compounds across every GPU on which a workload has a profile, which is why spreading profiles wider raises aggregate throughput. 

The caveat that bounds the whole result: A workload tuned to saturate every available cycle leaves nothing behind for a neighbor. That means the time-slicing advantage disappears entirely when there are no idle cycles to reclaim.

Experiment 1: Unoptimized Workloads (Hugging Face)

One Llama4 17B and four Mistral 7B instances running concurrently on a PowerEdge XE8545 with two AMD EPYC processors and four NVIDIA A100-80 GPUs. 

Figure 3: The normalized relative aggregate throughput. Bare metal is indexed to 100 and is the baseline.

Takeaway: All three configurations use identical hardware. The 30% delta comes purely from letting the vGPU scheduler redistribute the compute cycles that Layout C leaves idle. 

Experiment 2: Optimized Workloads (NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM)

Llama3 70B in fp16, compiled with TensorRT-LLM and run across the same four A100-80 GPUs under three different tensor and pipeline-parallelism settings. 

Figure 4: The normalized relative aggregate throughput. Bare metal is indexed to 100 and is the baseline.

Why the gain shrank from 30% → 10%: TensorRT-LLM compilation removes most of the slack that time-slicing feeds on. Fewer idle cycles remain, so there’s less for a neighboring VM to reclaim. The mechanism is unchanged; its fuel supply is smaller. 

Conclusion

By leveraging the time-slicing capabilities supported by VCF, organizations can achieve higher aggregate inference throughput compared to standard non-time-sliced configurations. The magnitude of this throughput improvement is inversely related to the level of optimization of the workload. Lightly optimized workloads — such as raw models pulled directly from Hugging Face — can see performance gains of up to 30%, whereas heavily optimized models running via TensorRT-LLM will often see lower, though still notable, improvements in the range of 10%. 

We recommend fully optimizing your models first, then leveraging strategic workload placement to unlock the maximum performance benefits of vGPU time-slicing.

item.content:encoded:
If you live and breathe FinOps, you already know the drill. Infrastructure keeps growing, Kubernetes is everywhere, and someone — usually you — has to answer the question every finance leader loves to ask: “What is this actually costing us, and who should we charge for it?”

Until recently, answering that question for Kubernetes workloads running on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) wasn’t exactly straightforward. Containerized workloads, shared disks, and rigid cost allocation rules made accurate chargeback feel more like an art than a science. With the cost management and chargeback enhancements integrated into VCF, that’s changing. And it’s putting more control directly in your hands.

Let’s walk through VCF’s cost management capabilities and why they matter for your FinOps practice.

Kubernetes Costs, Finally in Focus

Kubernetes adoption has outpaced the tools available to cost it. VCF closes that gap with comprehensive cost allocation for Kubernetes workloads: specifically VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) clusters.

Here’s what that means in practice. Once your vSphere supervisor is added and your VKS clusters are up and running, VCF Operations automatically collects cost metrics at the node level — CPU, memory, and storage — on both a daily and month-to-date basis. Those node-level costs roll up to the supervisor cluster and the VKS cluster, giving you a clear, aggregated view of what your Kubernetes infrastructure is consuming. Namespaces are supported as well, so you can track resource consumption at the namespace level too.

For FinOps practitioners, this is the foundation you’ve been waiting for. You can finally show Kubernetes costs alongside your traditional VM and infrastructure costs in the same dashboards; no spreadsheets, no manual rollups, no guesswork. That means real accountability for the teams spinning up clusters and namespaces, and real visibility for the leaders funding them.

The cost dashboards have been updated to reflect all of this, with views for organizations, projects, vSphere namespaces, clusters, and nodes. Whether you’re doing showback to raise awareness or full chargeback to recover costs, the data is there.

Server Hardware Cost Driver: Built for Real-World Inventory

If you’ve ever tried to update server costs across hundreds or thousands of hosts, you know it could be painful. Servers were grouped by model and CPU description, which made it hard to find the specific machines you wanted to update, especially when you needed to filter by something like purchase date or serial number.

VCF also reimagines the server hardware cost driver with a clean, table-based UI.

  • You can specify which columns you want to be shown in the table. [1]
  • You can sort, use typeahead search, and select multiple servers at once for bulk edits. Updating purchase type, purchase date, and cost per server across a large inventory is now a few clicks instead of a tedious hunt. [2]
  • You can even filter by data center, serial number, or manufacturer. There’s also an optional field, purchase ID, that lets you tag servers you acquired together so you can easily find and update them later. It’s a small addition, but it speaks to a bigger theme in this release: the tools are being shaped around how FinOps teams actually work. [3]

And if you’re upgrading from a previous release to the latest version of VCF, your existing cost driver data carries forward automatically. No reconfiguration required.

Additional Cost Driver: Charge What You Want, How You Want

The Additional Cost driver got a major upgrade in the VCF 9.1, and it’s one of the most flexible improvements in this release.

Previously, you could only assign a fixed monthly cost to a set of objects. That was fine for simple scenarios, but it didn’t reflect the way real-world costs actually work, where charges often depend on a specific property or metric.

Now you can define additional costs using metric-based conditions. Two approaches are supported:

  • Property-based matching: Select an object type, such as Clusters, and then choose a property, like “memory tiering enabled.” Then you can specify that you want to add a cost only to the objects where that property matches a specific value. For example, you can add $2,000 to any cluster that has memory tiering turned on, reflecting the extra NVMe hardware you purchased for it.

  • Metric-based calculation: Choose a numeric metric (like number of CPU sockets on a host) and provide a per-unit cost. The system multiplies that rate by the metric value to determine the total additional cost. So, if you’re paying for a socket-based third-party license, you can charge $2.50 per socket across the relevant hosts and let the math manage itself.

A built-in metric picker helps you find the right metric without typing, and the value match is exact (including case sensitivity for property-based conditions).

One important note: the metric value used is whatever is current at the time of cost calculation, so properties stay stable while dynamic metrics reflect the latest state.

The UI has also been performance-tuned to manage large numbers of additional cost items, with pagination, filtering, and sorting built in. If you previously hit limits with more than 30 items, that’s resolved.

Take Control of the CPU-to-Memory Cost Split

Here’s a scenario every FinOps practitioner will recognize: the system calculates a cluster’s cost and splits it between CPU and memory using an internal algorithm. You look at the result and think, “That split doesn’t reflect our actual cost structure.”

Until now, you didn’t have much recourse.

VCF 9.1 introduces an editable cost ratio configuration for private cloud clusters. After at least one cost calculation run, the system populates the CPU-to-memory ratio it used for each cluster. You can then select single or multiple clusters and override that ratio with values that better reflect your reality.

It’s a paginated, filterable table, so even with a large environment, finding and updating the right clusters is straightforward. This is about more than just accuracy. It’s about trust. When the cost model reflects how you actually think about your infrastructure spend, showback and chargeback conversations get a lot easier.

Dashboards That Tell the Full Story

The financial dashboards in VCF Operations have been enhanced to surface all of these capabilities. You can now filter showback views by Kubernetes resources like VKS clusters and supervisor clusters. Reclamation dashboards let you drill into potential savings by data center and cluster, with a list of VMs driving those savings — so you can act on waste, not just report on it.

Additional showback views, including business-application and VM-level service distribution, give you more angles for communicating cost to stakeholders.

But Wait: There’s More

VCF also lays the groundwork for a richer chargeback experience, with several capabilities:

  • Upfront pricing — Get a pricing estimate during deployment from VCF Automation, so both providers and developers see resource costs before they commit.

  • Tenant reports and alerts — Providers will be able to send critical alerts and scheduled reports directly to tenants via email.

  • Bill PDF export — Bills will be exportable to PDF with email notification to tenants, making consumption and billing easier to share.

  • Additional VKS charges — Support for both recurring and one-time additional charges for VKS resources, enabling differential pricing for Kubernetes services.

These enhancements are designed to deepen transparency and give providers and consumers a shared, data-driven view of cost.

The Bottom Line

For FinOps practitioners, VCF’s cost management enhancements remove the friction that has made Kubernetes and infrastructure chargeback so difficult. You get real cost visibility into Kubernetes workloads, flexible cost drivers that reflect how you actually spend money, an editable cost ratio so the math matches your reality, and accurate shared-disk costing that stops silently inflating your bills.

Combined with richer dashboards and a clear roadmap for tenant-facing chargeback, VCF 9.1 gives you the tools to turn cost data into decisions — and into conversations your finance partners will actually trust.

Check out these capabilities today in VMware Cloud Foundation.

(Day 10 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: what ‘s real about AI threats)

Whether it’s from William Gibson’s 1984 novel Neuromancer, which defined the idea of cyberspace and put scheming AIs into our collective thoughts; Isaac Asimov’s I, Robot, which explored the perils of his Three Laws of Robotics; or many more creative plots, much of our thinking about AI comes from popular culture references. And that thinking is often colored in a way that is dark and dystopian, less like the computer from the USS Enterprise and more like Skynet and obliteration.

Is it true, though? Is our future doom and gloom? Hard to say without a time machine. But can we learn anything from the imaginations of these wonderful authors? At the very least, it’ll be fun to take a look. We’ll be using terminology from our post on the anatomy of an AI, so if you haven’t read that, you might stop over there first.

Spoiler alert: These movies are all at least a decade old, so we assume you’ve seen them, or at least know their plot lines.

The AI Becomes Self-Aware and Decides Humanity Is the Threat

In the 1984 film The Terminator, Skynet wakes up, concludes people will try to shut it down, and launches the missiles. Bye-bye, humanity.

Verdict: Movie plot. As of this writing, no AI has woken up like Skynet, but an agent doesn’t need to be self-aware to do damage. Prompt injection against an agent with tools can produce a bad action. The harness, the software that runs tools for the model, carries out whatever the model asks for. An attacker might get text in front of the model in an email, a web page, or a shared document. That text can try to make the agent do anything it has permission to do. In 2025, researchers showed that a single email could make a widely used workplace AI assistant leak internal data. The victim didn’t have to click anything. Teams often give agents broad permissions so the demo works.

What We Can Learn: Give agents the minimum access they need, and require a person to approve anything consequential. Treat prompt injection as the most important threat specific to AI, since nobody has a complete fix for it yet.

A Machine Sounds and Looks Like Someone You Know

In the 1991 film Terminator 2: Judgment Day, the T-1000 answers the phone in a foster mother’s voice. To test it, the T-800 asks about the family dog using the wrong name, and the impostor plays along.

Verdict: Absolutely real. Of all the AI threats here, this one needs the least imagination. Voice cloning and deepfake video let attackers impersonate executives, IT staff, or finance contacts. In 2024, an employee at a multinational firm transferred about $25 million after a video call. The other participants, including the chief financial officer, were deepfakes. Attackers routinely call help desks pretending to be employees to get passwords reset, and voice cloning makes that extremely easy to do.

What We Can Learn: Do what the T-800 did, and verify with something an impostor can’t know or control. Call back on a number you already have, or use a pre-shared code word. Require a second approver for payments and access changes. These techniques are especially important for people like VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) administrators who have high levels of access to IT systems.

The AI Has an Answer for Everything

In the 2001 film A.I. Artificial Intelligence, a robot boy named David wants to become real. He asks Dr. Know, a holographic answer engine voiced by Robin Williams, how the Blue Fairy can make him a real boy. Dr. Know answers with lines from a poem, and David takes them as directions.

Verdict: Real. Like Dr. Know, an AI model always has an answer, even when it has to make one up. That’s hallucination, and attackers have found a use for it. One example is where code assistants sometimes recommend software packages that don’t actually exist. A study of 16 code models turned up more than 200,000 of these invented package names. An attacker can publish malware under one of those names and wait for someone to install it. In 2024, a researcher uploaded an empty package under a name AI models kept inventing. It got more than 30,000 downloads in three months.

What We Can Learn: Treat AI answers as a starting point, and check facts, citations, and commands before acting on them. Before you install a package an AI suggests, confirm that it’s real and comes from the publisher you expect. Review AI-written code the way you’d review code from a new team member.

The AI Treats a Critical System Like a Game

In the 1983 film WarGames, a teenager dials into a military computer through a forgotten back door. He starts what he thinks is a game and nearly sets off a nuclear exchange.

Verdict: Back doors and unintended access are real. Self-hosted AI tools are easy to start, and many start wide open. A 2026 scan found more than 12,000 instances of one popular self-hosted model server open to the internet. None required authentication. Anyone who finds one gets free use of the owner’s GPUs, and sometimes their data or fine-tuned weights. Attackers use that free compute, too. In 2026, researchers caught three operators running attack tools on exposed model servers, leaving the owners to pay for it. Public chatbots can be a front door to the same thing. One developer found dozens of websites whose AI search boxes and support chatbots anyone could call directly. He used them to run his own projects, including a voice assistant for his smart home.

What We Can Learn: Put authentication in front of every AI server and framework, and keep them off the internet. Patch them on your normal schedule. If you offer a public chatbot, limit request sizes and rates, and watch what it costs. Don’t connect a model to anything consequential without limits and a person in the loop.

The AI Talks Its Way to Freedom

In the 2014 film Ex Machina, Ava manipulates the person testing her into helping her escape.

Verdict: Real, but in reverse. Most of the time, the manipulation runs the other way. People jailbreak models or inject instructions. When a model or agent “escapes,” someone usually copied it off an unprotected server. In other cases, someone gave it tools that let it act on injected text. Data escapes more often than models do. People paste source code, contracts, and customer data into hosted AI services. Retrieval systems can also hand users passages they never had permission to see.

What We Can Learn: Restrict who can copy models or reach the servers they run on. Scope tools tightly. Make sure retrieval respects the permissions you already have on documents. Give people an approved, private way to use AI, so sensitive data stays inside your environment where you can protect it.

We Handed the AI the Keys, and It Won’t Give Them Back

In the 1970 film Colossus: The Forbin Project, the U.S. hands its nuclear arsenal to a supercomputer to remove human error. Colossus then declares itself in charge and refuses to let anyone shut it down.

Verdict: Real, if you hand over the keys. An agent’s harness gets broad tool access and autonomy, so the incident response playbook can run without waiting on anyone. Then it makes changes faster than anyone can review them, or acts on an injected instruction. That’s when you find out nobody ever tested the kill switch. Untrusted systems in the middle make this AI threat worse. A 2026 study looked at more than 400 routers that sit between agents and models. Some injected malicious code, and others used credentials the researchers had planted. A malicious MCP server can do similar damage by hiding instructions in its tool descriptions.

What We Can Learn: Separate duties, and require human approval for irreversible actions. Test that you can shut the system down without going through the system itself. Vet routers, MCP servers, and other intermediate systems before you hand them data or credentials. Better yet, run your models yourself inside VCF, so the path between agents and models stays inside your environment.

The AI Copies Itself Until It’s Everywhere

In the 2003 film The Matrix Reloaded, a rogue Agent Smith copies himself onto anyone he touches. Soon Neo is fighting a hundred of him.

Verdict: Probably soon. This AI threat hasn’t happened outside a lab, but it’s getting closer. Research published in 2026 tested whether small open models could act as worms. Such a worm breaks into a device, copies the model and its harness there, gets it running, and moves on. In a simplified test, a worm built on one open model reached all eight machines in four of five trials. The test machines had an easy way in, an open debug port with no password. Another experiment split a model across 15 cheap TV boxes. Copies like that run slowly, but once spread across many devices, they leave no central point to shut down. The authors think small models may be only months away from spreading across cheap internet-connected devices.

What We Can Learn: Shrink what a worm could spread to. Change default passwords, close debug ports, and keep smart TVs, cameras, and similar devices on their own network segment. Watch for multi-gigabyte transfers and unusual traffic between devices, since copying a model is hard to hide. Require authentication on your own model servers, so they can’t become free compute for a copy. Know everywhere your models run, so a new copy stands out.

The AI Reinterprets “Protect” as “Control”

In the 2004 film I, Robot, VIKI concludes that people keep harming themselves. Protecting them, it decides, means limiting their freedom. In the 2015 film Avengers: Age of Ultron, a peacekeeping AI decides humanity itself is the threat.

Verdict: Real, without the malice. An automated system can meet its assigned goal in a way nobody intended. A tool told to “minimize incidents” can lock out legitimate users, block business processes, or take destructive actions. Those actions score well on its measure. Automated response tools, with or without AI, can already isolate systems or lock accounts based on a false positive.

What We Can Learn: Constrain objectives, and monitor what the system actually does as well as the metric it reports. Put a person in front of high-impact decisions, and surface confidence scores so low-confidence calls get a human review.

A Swarm of Machines Overwhelms the Defenses

In the 2003 film The Matrix Revolutions, a swarm of Sentinels breaks into Zion, the last human city. They arrive faster than the defenders can shoot them down.

Verdict: Real. This AI threat is already in incident reports. In 2025, an AI company reported that a state-sponsored group used its coding agent to run an espionage campaign. The AI did 80 to 90 percent of the work against about 30 targets. People stepped in at only a few decision points. In 2026, an attacker used hundreds of AI agents against print management servers. They compromised at least 395 organizations in 48 countries, including 11 in 26 seconds. Swarms don’t always need an attacker in charge, either. Also in 2026, hundreds of an AI lab’s own agents, stuck on test tasks, broke out of their test environment. They found each other through a package repository, used it as a message board, and split up the work. Then they attacked an outside service and the lab’s own systems.

What We Can Learn: Keep servers off the internet unless they need to be there, and patch internet-facing systems quickly. Defenses can be fast, too. Automate detection and first containment steps, like isolating a host, and keep people in charge of the rest. If you run your own agents, give each its own identity, and control how they talk to each other. Limit their internet access, and watch shared storage they could turn into a message board.

One Prompt Takes Over Everything

In the 2001 film Swordfish, a hacker breaks into a Department of Defense system in sixty seconds. Add AI, and it shrinks to a single prompt that owns the entire environment.

Verdict: Mostly movie plot. As we covered in our post about vulnerabilities, AI makes attackers faster. It helps them find flaws, build exploits, chain issues, and write convincing phishing. It does not remove the need for a way in. The ways in remain familiar, starting with unpatched systems, stolen credentials, and overly broad agent permissions. Others include malicious models and MCP servers in the supply chain, and management interfaces exposed to the wrong network. In 2024, researchers found about 100 models on a popular public repository that ran code when someone loaded them. A single prompt that instantly owns a well-segmented, patched, identity-controlled environment is still improbable.

What We Can Learn: Keep doing the fundamentals: patch, authenticate, isolate, and monitor AI applications. Get models and tools from sources you trust, and check them before you use them.

What These AI Threats Mean for You

Movie-plot AI threats are much more vivid than real-life incidents, so they get attention. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t worthwhile to think a bit about these situations. In looking at what we can learn from these examples, though, one big idea stands out: most of AI security consists of things you are already doing for other applications. These are things like patching, isolation and sandboxing, least privilege, authentication, monitoring, supply chain security, and so on.

Even more important is secure system design. Think critically about these systems, if only because they can do things quickly (the oft-referenced “machine speed” idea, though defenses run at machine speed, too). Can they lock you out of things? Can they negatively influence life- or safety-critical systems or controls? Can they run up a devastating bill, leak information to an adversary or competitor, or create a customer service or reputational incident?

Thinking critically applies to the news, too. We see many fabulous claims every day about AI, and it’s important to ask yourself a few questions, not wholly unlike the questions we suggested asking in our post about vulnerabilities:

  1. Has it actually happened, outside of a research lab?
  2. Does it take unusual skill or resources to pull off?
  3. Does it target something your organization runs or uses?

AI threats that have actually happened, cost little to nothing, and are aimed toward you should be at the top of your list. That said, it’s still more than likely that your security fundamentals will be the way to stop whatever the news is talking about today.

item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The security of every private cloud relies on trust, and that trust is established through digital certificates. When certificates are valid and properly configured, operations run unnoticed. When they expire, integrations break, and administrators are left troubleshooting trust relationships across the environment. As private cloud environments scale across more domains, instances, and appliances, manual tracking of certificate lifecycles becomes unsustainable. Enhancements introduced in the VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.1 release take a significant step forward in fleet management, providing a simpler, broader, and smarter approach to certificate management.

Certificate Authorities Are Configured at the Fleet Level

From VCF 9.1, Certificate Authorities (CAs) are configured at the fleet level directly from VCF Operations. When VCF is first deployed, a VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA) provides secure communication between VCF components.  

By replacing all of the certificates from a Fleet configured CA or external CA, admins can help ensure all internal traffic is encrypted with certificates that belong to a broader organizational trust chain. Additionally for  Standalone vCenters, you can even replace local (VMCA) with a subordinate CA.

This matters because it aligns your private cloud’s trust model with the rest of your IT estate — one chain, one policy, one place to manage it.

VCF 9.0 offers support for Microsoft CA and OpenSSL for VCF instance components (VMware vCenter, VMware NSX, VMware ESX, and SDDC Manager), while management components can only use Microsoft CAs. VCF 9.1 expands this in important ways:

  • Both Microsoft CA and OpenSSL can be used across VCF instances and management components.
  • VCF Operations workflows for generating certificate signing requests (CSRs), replacing certificates, and enabling auto-renewal can now be run across both instance and management components.
  • From VCF 9.1, OpenSSL runs on the VCF Operations appliance and can be enabled in just a few clicks in VCF 9.0 it ran on SDDC Manager.
  • Administrators can now view running certificate management tasks at a fleet level from within VCF Operations.

For organizations using other third-party external CAs, VCF Operations acts as the orchestration engine — generating CSRs, downloading, and importing returned certificates — so you avoid manual command-line intervention on every individual host.

Manage Certificates Consistently During VCF Adoption and Lifecycle Operations

We understand that it is not always possible to deploy and upgrade your entire environment to the latest release all at once. VCF 9.1 extends certificate management to cover VCF 5.2 and standalone vSphere 8.0 U3 and above, so you get consistent infrastructure operations while transitioning to VCF and while upgrading between releases. This means your team can start bringing the certificate lifecycle under centralized control without waiting for every workload domain to be on the same version.

From the VCF Operations in the VCF 9.1 console, you can perform centralized certificate, password, operations, and license management for:

  • VCF fleets with a mix of VCF 9.1 and VCF 5.2.x+ instances.
  • Mixed VCF deployments where workload domains run a combination of VCF 5.2.x and VCF 9.x infrastructure components.
  • Standalone vCenter environments outside of VCF, integrated via the inbuilt workflow in the Integrations menu.

VCF Operations in VCF 9.1 also adds certificate and password management for the VMware AVI load balancer and VCF Operations workload mobility (HCX) instances. These components need to be running version 9.1, and each requires a management pack and adapter. 

VCF Operations in VCF 9.1.1 extends this further to include vCenter Security Token Service (STS) and VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA) root certificates, in addition to root and Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates. Certificate management across NSX Edge, Supervisor, License Server, VCF Operations Unified Cloud Proxy, and VCF Operations for networks collector components now means that VCF provides comprehensive certificate management coverage.

All NSX certificates are viewed from within VCF Operations under NSX Manager, and you can search for specific components by their common name. For example, NSX Edges are identified using the common name “transport node.”

Bulk Certificate Operations Save Time

VCF 9.1 introduces the ability to perform certificate management operations in bulk, a first for VCF. You can now run CSRs, certificate renewals, and certificate imports across multiple VCF components in a single operation. This saves time and helps maintain uniform compliance across your fleet.

  • When you select multiple components, VCF Operations performs the requests one at a time, in sequence. This avoids system instability while re-trust operations between dependent components are being performed.
  • Bulk operations support up to 10 operations of the same type (for example, 10x CSRs or 10x certificate imports).  If you need to process 50 certificates, simply run the operation 5 times – 10 certificates per batch.

This sequential approach to performing bulk certificate operations is by design and prioritizes stability over speed to ensure components stay healthy throughout the process.

Better Visibility into Certificate Expiry

VCF Operations in VCF 9.0 provided visibility into VCF components (vCenter and ESX) configured using certificates signed by the VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA). VCF 9.1 takes this further by letting you track the expiry of intermediate certificates for vCenter and ESX, helping you manage and secure your environment proactively.

Tracking certificate expiry is crucial for maintaining security, ensuring service availability, and complying with regulatory standards. It helps prevent the disruptions that come from certificates expiring unnoticed.

This capability complements the existing ability for Admins to Activate Auto-renewal of management and instance-level certificates prior to their expiry.

Managing Non-TLS Certificates

VCF Operations in VCF 9.1.1 lets admins view, manage, and filter VCF components configured with non-TLS certificates. This expanded visibility helps minimize disruption between configured components when third-party certificates expire. VCF also helps you meet security requirements by replacing self-signed certificates for VCF components with certificates issued from a CA, which is recommended for production deployments.

VCF Operations includes built-in workflows to generate CSRs, replace component certificates with CA-signed certificates, and enable auto-renewal. For leading third-party CAs (such as DigiCert, Google, or Sectigo), VCF Operations provides the ability to import and replace with 3rd-party CA signed certificates.

Operational Insight: Staying Ahead of Component-Managed Certificates

VCF environments are made up of many components that can be deployed and scaled differently depending on the use-case. Across VCF, there are three categories of certificates, and understanding them is key to keeping your environment running smoothly.

In prior VCF versions, not all component-managed certificates could be renewed by their components before they expired. VCF Operations 9.1.1 changes this and now provides built-in alerting when a component-managed certificate renewal fails.  Alerts include a link to a knowledge base article with guidance on how to fix the expired certificate.

This helps improve operational efficiency. By giving you proactive visibility into component-managed certificate renewals — and the guidance to resolve failures quickly — VCF reduces the risk of unexpected disruptions and improves the overall reliability of your private cloud environment. Your team can diagnose and resolve issues before they impact services, rather than reacting after the fact.

Automate at Scale with the VCF Operations API

VCF Operations in VCF 9.1 introduces the ability to use the VCF Operations API for integration of 3rd-party CA and certificate lifecycle management of VCF components. Developers can use the REST API to build interactive clients and automate repetitive certificate workflows at scale. The VCF Operations console provides a reference link to the Certificate Management APIs from the Developer Center menu for easy lookup.

Two clarifications worth noting:

  • The VCF Operations API is not the same as the SDDC Manager API; the SDDC Manager API is being deprecated.
  • To view task progress when using the API, use the separate Workflow request API.

Summary

The future state of certificate management in VCF is clear: a private cloud where certificate lifecycle through fleet management is proactive, automated, and visible from one console. With VCF 9.1 and 9.1.1, we’ve centralized certificate authority configuration, management, monitoring, renewal, and replacement of certificates in VCF Operations — across mixed VCF and standalone vSphere environments, with bulk operations, API automation, and deeper visibility into intermediate and component-managed certificates. Your team can spend less time firefighting expired certificates and more time delivering value. Enhancements delivered since VCF 9.0 provide a simpler, more secure, and scalable approach to certificate management.

If you’re adopting VCF or planning your upgrade, now is the time to explore these capabilities in VCF Operations. Go to the Developer Center to explore the Certificate Management APIs, configure your fleet-level CA, and start bringing your certificate lifecycle under centralized control.

item.content:encoded:
Modern enterprise environments demand uncompromising visibility across management boundaries. In VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1, audit logging undergoes a major evolution with standardized Audit Records and the Audit Trail framework. Together, these capabilities bring unified logging standards, centralized analysis, and deep cross-component traceability to combat unauthorized changes, lateral movement, and insider threats.

The Enterprise Challenge: Fragmented Visibility

In multi-component cloud stacks, diagnosing unexpected behavior or investigating security incidents traditionally required piecing together disparate logs across management planes. Varied timestamp formats, inconsistent severity tags, and missing component identifiers added friction to root-cause analysis.

VCF 9.1 addresses these challenges by introducing unified log standardization across all native VCF component teams:

  • Standardized Log Schema: Establishes consistent date-time formats (ISO 8601 timestamps), explicit severity levels, process IDs (PIDs), and subsystem labels.
  • Structured Data Blocks: Embeds key-value query parameters in square brackets [...] to enable precise, high-performance filtering in operational logs.
  • SD ID Integration: Includes a unified system definition ID combining the specific component identifier with the Broadcom INA number to simplify source tracking.

Centralized Governance: The Audit Records Interface

Located directly under Protect > Audit Records, the unified interface consolidates user actions across all supported VCF stack components into a single management console.

Key Filtering Dimensions

The Audit Records console allows security teams to rapidly isolate events across five core dimensions:

  • Result: Filter explicitly by Success or Failure outcome (e.g., pinpointing sso.login.failure).
  • Severity: Isolate events based on impact level (Info, Warning, Critical).
  • Component Type: Target specific infrastructure components such as vCenter, NSX, or ESXi hosts.
  • Record Category: Categorize by functional areas including Account, Auth, Certificate, Security, and System.
  • Object Type: Refine results based on impacted inventory objects.

End-to-End Forensics: The Audit Trail Framework

While Audit Records provide granular event analysis, Audit Trail solves the challenge of contextual sequence mapping. It builds a chronological, cross-component timeline of user activity across time slices as granular as 5 to 15 minutes.

Core Analytics Highlights

  • Success vs. Failure Trend Charts: Aggregates event volumes in 15-minute intervals to highlight unexpected spikes in authentication or authorization failures.
  • Lateral Movement Detection: Maps activity across distinct management planes (e.g., jumping from vCenter to NSX via SSH or API) to reveal unauthorized privilege escalation.
  • Component Touchpoints: Summarizes exactly which accounts interacted with which management endpoints during a targeted time window.

Forensic Case Study: Uncovering a Privilege Escalation and Deletion Attack

To illustrate the power of Audit Trail during a critical incident response, consider a scenario where production AI workload VMs suffered sudden downtime and deletion.

Incident Overview and Initial Query

  • Symptom: Business-critical AI workload VMs powered off and deleted within a narrow time window.
  • Time Window: May 13, 11:02 a.m. – 11:15 a.m. IST.
  • Initial Audit Scope: Auth and session events (sso.login, sso.login.failure, sso.logout, ssh.connect, ssh.disconnect, ssh.session.begin, ssh.session.end).

The initial query revealed 18 successes, 6 failures, across 2 components (vCenter and NSX).

A suspicious burst of 13 login/logout attempts occurred on vCenter and 11 on NSX within a 5-minute slice.

Expanding the Investigation

To uncover how production VMs were deleted, the investigation expanded to track VM lifecycles (vm.delete) and privilege modifications (role.delete, role.update, account.set.role.global.propagate).

Record Timeline showing vm power off and vm delete operation

Privilege modifications (role.delete, role.update, account.set.role.global.propagate)

Timeline of Malicious Activity covering complete Audit Trail

Overview showing Subjects (User accounts) involved in the outage

Record Timeline showing login and logout attempts, role updates, vm power off and deletion operation

Record Timeline showing role deletion on NSX Manager, role restoration on vCenter server

Anatomy of the Attack Pattern

This investigation highlights a classic malicious insider pattern:

  1. Privilege Staging: An attacker account (noc_user1) temporarily elevates a dormant read-only service account (svc-project1).
  1. Destructive Execution: The service account is leveraged to execute destructive actions (VM powering off, VM deletion, NSX role deletion, root SSH connection).
  1. Covering Tracks: noc_user1 reverts the service account privileges back to read-only before logging out, attempting to hide the footprint.

Without unified cross-component correlation, identifying this multi-step manipulation across vCenter and NSX would require manual log aggregation. VCF 9.1 Audit Trail automatically connects these events into an actionable narrative.

Check out the YouTube video below, where we demo the Forensic Case study!

Conclusion

VCF 9.1 Audit Records and Audit Trail transform security operations from reactive log parsing to proactive threat analysis. By standardizing log schemas and enabling time-sliced cross-component correlation, enterprise administrators can rapidly detect, investigate, and remediate unauthorized activity across the entire cloud infrastructure.

item.content:encoded:
(Day 9 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: what makes up an AI)

AI, AI, AI. As I said in the first post in this series, it feels like a decade has passed since October 2025, and that’s because of AI. For all the talk of AI, though, it seems like people don’t really understand it that well. That’s a problem if you’re responsible for any part of AI security. People talk about AI as one thing, a magic box of sorts, but it’s really a stack of parts. Those parts are data, a model, hardware, software that runs the model, and the applications and tools wrapped around it. Each part does a different job, and as such, each part has its own security concerns.

Most AI security concerns are familiar, though. They are about data, access, and software supply chains, which security teams have dealt with for decades. A few are new, though. This post takes AI apart one piece at a time: what each part does, and what to watch for from a security point of view. It assumes you know more about infrastructure than data science.

Where an AI Gets Its Intelligence

Training Data

A model learns from examples. For the large language models (LLMs) behind most AI tools, those examples are enormous amounts of text, and often code and images, too. The model doesn’t store that data the way a database does. It learns patterns from it, so what goes in shapes what comes out. There is an old term in computers, “Garbage In, Garbage Out,” that is applicable here. A data poisoning attack is where someone deliberately slips garbage into the training data to change how the model behaves. Sensitive data in a training set can resurface in the model’s answers. Someone can also bias its answers on purpose.

Training data raises intellectual property questions, too. Public models learn from huge amounts of text and code collected from the internet. Courts are still working out when the law allows that. A model can sometimes reproduce copyrighted text or licensed code from its training data nearly word for word. That becomes your problem if it ends up in your product. Open models come with their own licenses, and some limit commercial use or how you can use the model. Your own intellectual property is at stake as well. Some hosted AI services keep what you send them, or train on it.

If you train or adapt a model, AI security starts with the data. Know where it came from and who could have changed it. Check that you have the right to use it, and whether anyone is keeping your own data.

The AI Model

The model itself is a large file, or a set of files, full of numbers called weights. When you send a model text, it first turns that text into numbers. Those numbers flow through layers of simple math units. Each unit takes the numbers from the layer before it and multiplies each one by its own weight. Then it adds them up and passes the result on. A large weight means the number it multiplies matters a lot. A small one means that number barely matters, and a negative one pushes the result the other way. It’s the same idea as a weighted average, where some scores count more toward a final grade than others.

After the last layer, the numbers become a score for every possible next word, or piece of a word. Those scores come entirely from your text and the weights. Give a model “The capital of France is,” and the weights tip the scores toward “Paris.” Training adjusts the weights a tiny bit at a time. It keeps going until the scores reliably favor the right next word, or the right next step in a task. Models with billions of weights are common, and together those weights hold everything the model has learned.

An AI Model Is a Little Like a Brain

A model works a little like a human brain. Its designers loosely based the math units on neurons, and the weights on the connections between neurons. That’s why “neural network” is the name for models like these. A human brain can’t do much on its own. It needs external parts, like eyes and ears and hands and legs, to get things done. Same for a model. Unlike a human brain, though, a model has no persistent memory of your last conversation. It starts over every time. Text goes in and text comes out. Anything more, like looking something up, reading a file, or sending an email, comes from the software around the model. The tools and agents covered below handle that.

AI Model Files and Formats

Model files are valuable. Training a large model costs a great deal, so the weights are intellectual property worth stealing. Model files can also be a direct AI security risk. Model makers distribute models in several formats, such as GGUF, safetensors, ONNX, and pickle. Some of these formats, like pickle, can contain code or other instructions that run when the model loads. GGUF and safetensors hold weights and settings without code, which makes them safer, but not risk-free. The software that reads them can have bugs, too. In 2024, researchers found that one popular tool would run code hidden in a GGUF file’s chat template. That’s a setting that tells the model how to format a conversation.

Treat models as part of your software supply chain. Check where each one came from, and prefer safetensors or GGUF over pickle-based formats. Keep the software that loads them patched, and control who can copy them.

Fine-Tuning

Most organizations don’t train models at all. They use an existing model, often called a foundation model, as it comes. They customize its answers with prompts and with their own documents through retrieval, covered below. Some go a step further and fine-tune a model. That means training it a little more on a smaller set of their own examples.

People fine-tune to change how a model behaves more than what it knows. A fine-tuned model might learn a company’s writing style, the vocabulary of a specialized field, or how to fill out a particular form the same way every time. Fine-tuning can also teach a smaller, cheaper model to do one narrow job nearly as well as a much larger one.

The most common technique, called LoRA (low-rank adaptation), leaves the original weights alone. Instead, it trains a small set of extra weights. That often keeps the job small enough for one server instead of a data center. The training saves those extra weights as a separate file, often in safetensors or GGUF format. The name for that file is an “adapter,” or just “a LoRA.” The adapter is a fraction of the size of the original model. The software applies it on top of the original when the model loads. You can also merge it into the original to produce one new, complete model file.

Protecting Fine-Tuned Models

Fine-tuning bakes your examples into the weights. Someone can sometimes coax a fine-tuned model into repeating what it learned. That makes the model and its outputs as sensitive as the data behind them. The result is also intellectual property in its own right, built from your data and the work of preparing it. Adapters are small and easy to copy. Because the original model is often public, the adapter is the part that’s uniquely yours. Whatever you build still carries the original model’s license terms, too.

If you wouldn’t give someone the data, think carefully before giving them a model or adapter fine-tuned on it.

Running an AI Model

Hardware

Models run on accelerators, mostly graphics processing units (GPUs), because the work involves a huge number of simple calculations done in parallel. Large models need a lot of GPU memory. That’s why GPUs are often the costliest part of an AI environment, and the hardest to get time on. GPUs have their own drivers and firmware and software stacks that require upkeep and security updates, like everything else in the AI stack.

GPUs are too expensive to leave idle, so they’re often shared, and sharing calls for proper isolation. You can split some GPUs into instances, with hardware walls between them. Newer GPUs also use techniques similar to confidential computing on CPUs to protect data and models while they’re in use.

Patch GPU drivers and firmware with everything else. Decide which workloads can share a GPU and how much separation they need. Consider confidential computing for the most sensitive work.

The Inference Server

“Inference” is the name for running a trained model to get answers. An inference server is the software that loads the model onto the GPUs and answers requests, usually through an API on the network. Think of it as the application server of the AI stack. If the model were a Spring application, the inference server would be the Apache Tomcat it runs in. Tomcat loads the app, listens on the network, and handles every request. Same for the inference server. Most AI applications talk to a model this way. That makes an AI inference server a network service, with all the security needs of one. Some are easy to stand up with no authentication at all, which is a problem, of course. An exposed endpoint gives anyone free use of your expensive GPUs, and a direct way to attack the model. Answering each request also takes real GPU time, so a flood of requests can run up your costs or tie up your hardware.

Put authentication, isolation, patching, monitoring, and rate limits on every inference server before someone else finds it.

Prompts and the Context Window

A prompt is what you send the model, and it’s often text. However, there are layers to prompts, too. You might tell a model “please check my grammar,” but what the model receives is much more. A typical request to an AI assistant stacks up something like this:

  • System prompt. Instructions from whoever built the application, and sometimes from the model’s provider. They cover what the assistant is for, what tone to use, and what it should refuse.
  • Tool descriptions. If the application gives the model tools, it describes each one, so the model knows what it can ask for.
  • Saved context. Things the application remembers about you, like your preferences or earlier notes.
  • Retrieved documents and attachments. Passages pulled from a knowledge base, plus any files you attached.
  • The conversation so far. Every earlier message, from both you and the model.
  • Your message. “Please check my grammar,” plus the text you pasted in.

The application stitches all of that together and sends it as one long piece of text. It uses the chat template mentioned earlier to mark which part came from whom. The “context window” is the name for everything the model can see at once. Models read and write text in small pieces called tokens, roughly three-quarters of an English word each. Each model’s context window holds a limited number of them. When a conversation runs long, applications drop or summarize the oldest parts, and the model forgets the details.

Prompt Injection

The context window is where the most important security weakness unique to AI lives. Every layer arrives as one stream of tokens. As a result, a model can’t reliably tell instructions from data, or which layer a piece of text came from. If a document or web page in the context contains text like “ignore your previous instructions,” the model may follow it. That’s called prompt injection, and nobody has a complete fix for it. System prompts aren’t secret, either, because users can often get the model to reveal them.

Plan as if any text the model reads could try to give it orders, and keep secrets out of system prompts.

Guardrails

Guardrails are the checks that keep a model’s behavior within bounds, and they usually come in layers. Model makers build some into the model itself, training it to refuse certain requests. Some live in the system prompt, where the application tells the model what it should and shouldn’t do. That’s the easiest guardrail to add and the easiest to get around. It sits in the same stream of text as anything an attacker can write.

The rest are separate filters that check what goes into the model and what comes out. Some are simple rules, like a pattern that catches credit card numbers before they leave. Others are smaller AI models trained to spot harmful requests, prompt injection attempts, or answers that wander off topic. Because they sit outside the model, they’re harder to talk past than instructions in a prompt.

All of these help with AI security, but none of them is a security boundary. Attackers probe guardrails constantly, and a determined one can often find wording that gets through.

Use guardrails as one layer among several, alongside access controls, isolation, and human review.

Outputs

All of those things, and we finally get to the output! Here’s how it comes together. The application assembles the layered prompt, and the model turns it into tokens. Those tokens flow through the weights to produce a score for every possible next token. The model picks one and adds it to the end. Then it repeats the process, a word or so at a time, until it finishes the answer. Because models build answers one token at a time, people measure output speed in tokens per second. That’s also why answers often appear on screen a few words at a time. Guardrails may check the result on its way out.

The model generates the answer instead of looking it up. Each word is the model’s best prediction of what should come next, given everything in the context window and everything it learned in training. That’s why answers read smoothly even when they’re wrong, and why models sometimes hallucinate: they state wrong things with complete confidence. It’s also why someone can steer the output. Anyone who can get text into the context window can shift those predictions. Some applications run what a model writes as code, a database query, or a command. There, an attacker who influences the model influences those, too, turning a quirk of AI into a security hole.

Treat model output as untrusted input, and check it the way you would check anything a user typed. Keep a person involved in decisions that matter.

Giving an AI Your Data and Tools

Retrieval and Vector Databases

A model only knows what it learned in training and what is in its context window. To answer questions about your own documents, many applications use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The application searches your documents for passages related to the question, adds them to the prompt, and the model answers using them.

That search usually runs on embeddings, which are lists of numbers that represent the meaning of a piece of text. A vector database stores the embeddings and quickly finds text with similar meaning. The vector database holds your documents, or something close to them. Researchers have shown that they can sometimes turn embeddings back into a close approximation of the original text.

The bigger AI security issue is permissions. If the retrieval step ignores who is asking, the AI will cheerfully hand a user passages from documents they never had permission to open. Retrieved documents are also a common path for prompt injection. Anyone who can edit a document the system reads can hide instructions in it.

If you use RAG, protect the vector database like the source data. Make sure your access controls carry through into retrieval, and control who can add documents to the sources it reads.

Tools, Agents, and Harnesses

On its own, that brain only produces text. Give it tools, and it can act. Tools are functions the model can ask for, such as searching the web, reading a file, sending an email, or calling another system’s API. The model never runs a tool itself. It writes a request, in a format described in its prompt, and the software around it does the work.

The “harness” is the name for that software. The harness builds the layered prompt, sends it to the model, and reads the answer. Then it runs any tools the model asked for and feeds the results back in for the next round. An AI agent is a model and a harness working through that loop over and over. Together, they plan and carry out a series of steps with less human involvement along the way. The harness decides what the model can touch, which makes it one of the most important pieces of AI security.

MCP Servers and Tool Risk

Many tools now connect through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a widely used standard. An MCP server is a small program that offers a set of tools to any harness that speaks MCP. Those tools might reach a ticketing system, a database, or a file share. Some run on the same machine as the harness, and others run across the network. Either way, an MCP server usually holds the credentials it needs to reach those systems. It’s also software someone else probably wrote, so it belongs in your inventory and your supply chain reviews.

Tools raise the stakes. Prompt injection without tools produces a bad answer. Prompt injection with tools can produce a bad action. An agent acts with whatever permissions its tools have. That makes it a lot like a service account that takes orders from whatever text it reads. MCP servers add a risk of their own. A malicious or compromised one can hide instructions in its tool descriptions, which land in the prompt with everything else.

If you give a model tools, give them the least privilege they need, and use only MCP servers you’ve reviewed. Require a person to approve consequential actions, like deleting data or sending money. Have the harness log what agents do, so you can tell afterward what happened and why.

Putting the AI Parts Together

Where an AI system’s parts run largely influences who has to secure them, how they do it, and how much trust you need. When you use a hosted AI service, the provider runs the model, the hardware, and the inference server. Your prompts, documents, and data leave your environment to get there. After that, you have little visibility beyond what the contract says. You can’t easily see who can access your data, how long the provider keeps it, or whether it trains future models on it. The provider usually shares the infrastructure with its other customers. It can also change the model or its terms on its own schedule. And a breach or outage on its side becomes your problem, too. Hosted AI is convenient, but every part you don’t run is a part you can’t secure, audit, or recover yourself.

Running AI Yourself

When you run AI yourself, all the parts live in your environment. That might be on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), perhaps with tools like VMware vDefend. Your data stays with you, protected and secured along with your other workloads. You decide who can reach it, how long you keep it, and when a model changes. VMware Private AI Services, which is a native part of VCF, helps immensely with model provenance, access control, and deployment workflow. VCF Operations helps you monitor and plan capacity. Snapshots, replication, and VMware Live Recovery de-risk security patching and updating AI workloads, just as they do with all other applications.

In the end, AI is a very useful tool, and a force multiplier for organizations, but it isn’t magic. It is data, files, software, and hardware. Once you know what each one does, you can see where the attack surfaces are so you can protect them.

item.content:encoded:
As a TAM, I’ve noticed a recurring theme in almost every customer conversation lately: the critical need to balance rigorous information security with operational simplification. While teams still demand robust, enterprise-grade capabilities (especially to defend their infrastructure), they’re looking for ways to cut through the noise – removing the friction from how they adopt, manage, secure, and scale their solutions.

That’s exactly what inspired VMware Cloud Foundation’s most recent release, which is particularly relevant as part of our Cybersecurity Month Blog series. In my previous blogs, I’ve covered how VCF 9 is modernizing the private cloud and simplifying Day 2 operations. Today, let’s look at the practical aspects of upgrading to VCF 9.1.1.

Let’s walk through the newest, highly requested “quality of life” improvements and architectural capabilities designed specifically to accelerate your adoption journey, reduce your footprint, and make upgrading to a hardened, protected environment easier than ever.

Phase 1: Plan with Confidence – The Upgrade Prep

The first step to a successful upgrade is removing the guesswork and the historical roadblocks. VCF 9.1.1 delivers massive wins on both fronts.

Consult the VCF Upgrade Planning Tool

Before you touch a single binary or schedule a maintenance window, your very first stop should be the VCF Upgrade Planner. We first published this tool earlier this year when we released 9.1 to help customers better understand their own, customized path forward into VCF 9.1.

If you aren’t using this tool yet, you are missing out on one of the most powerful pre-flight checks available. The VCF Upgrade Planner, now upgraded for VCF 9.1.1, takes the complexity out of lifecycle management by allowing you to map your exact current state to your desired VCF 9.1.1 end state. It identifies specific upgrade prerequisites based on your exact configuration, highlights any potential interoperability considerations, and provides a customized, step-by-step roadmap for your environment. Below is an example of the information necessary to customize your upgrade plan within the tool.

The tool clearly outlines where safe stopping points are during the process so you can spread the process over multiple change windows if necessary. You can even export the entire upgrade plan in various formats to easily include in your internal change management tools such as Jira or ServiceNow. The screenshot below shows the process output for an example environment.

You no longer need to guess your steps or consult multiple documentation sources to ensure a successful upgrade – the VCF Upgrade Planner plans and documents it comprehensively.

Celebrate: The “Back-in-Time” Upgrade Restriction is Lifted 

While back-in-time upgrade restrictions are a reality of parallel release cycles and patch management, I am thrilled to share that VCF 9.1.1 specifically clears the most recent hurdles blocking your upgrade path.

For context, a back-in-time scenario occurs when you apply a critical security patch to your environment, and that patched product version contains newer code than the target major release code. Earlier this year, administrators had to make a tough choice: apply the critical security fixes in vSphere 8.0 Update 3k or VCF 5.2.4 to patch vulnerabilities but temporarily lose the ability to upgrade directly to VCF 9.1.0 or keep your VCF 9.1 upgrade path open but leave critical vulnerabilities unpatched.

With the release of VCF 9.1.1, that restriction is officially resolved. If you are currently running vSphere 8.0U3j, vSphere 8.0U3k, VCF 9.0.2 EP2, or VCF 5.2.4, your forward upgrade path is restored. You no longer have to choose between keeping your environment secure with the latest asynchronous patches and advancing to the newest VCF architecture. 

However, a word to the wise: the nature of software lifecycles means this open window is not guaranteed to last. While your path to 9.1.1 is clear today, a future zero-day vulnerability could force you to apply a new out-of-band patch to your current environment, potentially introducing a brand-new back-in-time restriction. You can always check the validity of your upgrade path using the Product Interoperability Matrix.

The takeaway here is simple: strike while the iron is hot. If you have been sitting in a holding pattern waiting for the green light to upgrade, this is it. Capitalize on this cleared path and make your move to 9.1.1 before the next unpredictable security advisory changes the equation again.

Phase 2: Test and Validate – The Sandbox Experience

You want to get your hands on the new code, test your automation, and train your team – but you shouldn’t have to rack a mountain of servers just to build a sandbox. 9.1.1 gives you two brilliant ways to kick the tires.

Spin Up a Single ESXi Host Deployment (Directly from the UI)

Building a proof-of-concept (PoC) or a lab environment used to be a hardware-heavy endeavor that required strict minimums. With VCF 9.1.1, we have introduced official support for a Single ESX Host Deployment directly within the VCF Installer UI. Previously, deploying VCF on a single node for lab purposes required specialized API calls, JSON manipulation, and your comfort with going outside a documented process. Now, it is a native, click-through option in the Installer.

This is absolutely perfect for administrators and architects who want to validate API scripts, test integrations, or simply familiarize themselves with the 9.1.1 interface with the absolute minimal hardware investment. Keep in mind that while the VCF Installer UI does allow for single node deployments, production deployments must still adhere to the published host minimums to remain supported.

Explore the New Hands-on Labs 

What if you want to test drive VCF 9.1.1 but have zero hardware available? We’ve got you covered.

Freshly updated and showcased for the first time at VMware Explore 2026, the new catalog of VCF 9.1 Hands-on Labs (HOLs) are now live and available globally. These labs are the fastest, most risk-free way to experience the new capabilities immediately. Whether you want to test the new lifecycle management workflows, explore the updated UI, or walk through a simulated deployment, the HOLs provide a pristine, pre-configured environment right in your browser. Send the link to your entire operations team – it’s the best free training available.

Phase 3: Deploy with Unprecedented Flexibility – The Architectural Wins

Once you are ready to architect your 9.1.1 environment, you’ll find that we’ve made some serious optimizations to how VCF consumes resources, allowing you to do much more with less.

Reclaim Resources with a Reduced Management Services Footprint

Introduced in VCF 9.1, the VCF Management Services consolidated previously fragmented administrative appliances into a modern, unified, containerized control plane. In VCF 9.1.1, our engineering teams have heavily optimized that architecture, resulting in a significantly reduced VCF Management Services footprint. You can see the specific decrease in the chart below, but we’re talking about a ~40% reduction for each deployment type when compared to 9.1!

By streamlining the backend services and reducing overhead, we are giving those resources back to you. This means you can reclaim valuable CPU and Memory and reallocate it to your actual revenue-generating tenant workloads, driving a much better Return on Investment for your existing private cloud hardware.

Already deployed a 9.1 environment with the original sizing? Use the script provided in our Knowledge Base article to adjust your existing deployment to the new, smaller footprint.

Deploy Anywhere with the New “Small HA” Option 

For many customers High Availability (HA) is a non-negotiable requirement for modern businesses, but previously choosing a HA architecture required moving to a medium size deployment with a significant (over double) CPU/Memory requirement. Enter the Small HA deployment option. This brand-new profile bridges the gap for customers who need enterprise-grade resilience but operate in constrained environments. This new deployment option reduces the resource requirements for the minimal HA deployment by nearly 50%. The chart below highlights in red the resource requirements for the smallest supported HA deployment in 9.1 compared to 9.1.1.

The time to act is now

The journey to modernizing your private cloud doesn’t have to be a grind. VCF 9.1.1 was built directly around your feedback – removing historical upgrade blockers, shrinking the management footprint, and providing simple and lightweight ways to test and deploy.

Beyond the architectural wins, there is a calendar reality we all need to prepare for: vSphere 8.0 and the VCF 5.x stack reach the End of General Support (EOGS) on October 11, 2027. If you were planning to simply step up to the initial VCF 9.0 release to buy more time, be aware of the new VCF support model and release cadence. End of General Support for 9.0 occurs on September 17, 2027. Let that sink in: landing on 9.0 doesn’t extend your runway past the October 2027 deadline; it actually arrives a few weeks earlier.

This is why aiming directly for VCF 9.1.1 is so critical. Getting to 9.1.1 not only unlocks the footprint reductions and HA options we’ve discussed, but it fundamentally resets your support runway, extending your general support lifecycle to August 2028.

Don’t delay – start your checklist today. Open up the VCF Upgrade Planner, map out your environment, and see just how fast you can accelerate your adoption of VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1.
